utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I was informed that the Defence would like to address the Chamber. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if it is something that should be dealt with before we start with the next witness, please proceed, otherwise, I would like you to wait until the witness has testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, it should be done before the next witness. Also, it could be done after the witness, but I propose to do a kind of grouping so that we -- so that we gain time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...after the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second part will be done after the witness, but before you decide on the question of the transcripts, a decision need to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had some difficulties in following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have difficulties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would like to address us in respect of the transcript or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two problems, Mr. President. One will concern the witness testimony of this witness and the second one will be the problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So just on the following witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...if you could do that in one or two minutes, then we can do it the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. Mr. President, in respect of the witness who is about to appear, it seems on the basis of the statements that we have, this witness who will be called to testify on the incidents of shelling, that is on the Markale market incident. The Defence is in a critical position because it would have liked to ask a whole line of questioning in respect of the manipulations that we called either in the press or in the manipulations of the pieces, and I am talking about the pieces, exhibits, that concern Markale, but we don't know what your decision will be. Because you know that there has been some time we have asked for your Chamber to pass a decision to reject, to exclude, these exhibits. Because we do not have your decision and because we don't know what it will be, we don't know whether we should waste time, perhaps uselessly, on a matter that will have no sense if you are going to reject these exhibits since they have all been manipulated. That is a practical point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The exhibits you are talking about were the -- could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am talking about all the medical pieces that may have been subjected to "grattage" or any kind of manipulation, and we are in a delicate position if we want to respect the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will give you -- as far as the "grattage" is concerned, we will let you know exactly what exhibits, what decision will be taken by the Chamber. We will do that after the first break. We will start with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can I go about another matter or shall I go on -- do it later? Thank you very much. Now, in respect of the transcript, Mr. President, we gave it a fair bit of thought and we established that as far as the yellow pads are concerned, and I believe that the yellow pads will not do, and therefore I believe that, on the part of the Defence, there is a strong will to limit ourselves to the essential. The two transcripts should be equivalent, must be equivalent to each other, and both parties should be careful of this. Yesterday, you saw that we really essentially intervened when there were things that didn't match in a flagrant way, and the reason why we seem to be doing it more, it is purely for linguistic reasons, but really the Defence doesn't mind if Prosecution has another polyglot on their side who will be doing this work. Another thing, Mr. President, it seems almost impossible that this work is done at the end of hearing, for the simple reason that we would actually waste more time, lose more time, because we would have to return to something that happened one or two hours previously. We would have to refresh the memory of a witness, or perhaps even of the Judges or the two parties. It would be a lot wiser to be done when it has to be done at that time. But, obviously, we will try and keep to the essential. I do not see any other solutions, and I am very sorry about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I accept that my friend believes that his interjections yesterday were only on important matters. The fact is, there were 12 interjections, which is unsatisfactory from the point of view of the flow of evidence. What I propose does not deprive him of the opportunity of making his important corrections. It simply relates to the time in which it is done. And my submission is that when the questioner and the witness in the box speak the same language, then there is no reason why the corrections cannot be made at the end of that day's testimony. Where the witness speaks a different language to the questioner, and secondly, where the interjection relates to the translation of the question to the witness's language, in those circumstances, it would be appropriate, in my respectful submission, for the correction to be made on the spot. But, otherwise, they could wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace, what about problems in the translation of the answers because if, for example, the witness speaks French and if the translation into English would be confusing, then would that not be a reason? Otherwise, you might be deprived from a proper understanding of what the witness testified about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, to the extent that that concern would reflect adversely on the Prosecution, the Prosecution's understanding, I would still be prepared for those corrections to be made at the end of the day's testimony, or at least at the end of the witness's testimony, rather than during the testimony. It is a balancing act. And when one compared the losses, I think that the impact which the present practice is having on examination-in-chief is so severe that the course I respectfully propose is preferable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Just on the issue raised by Mr. Ierace of the questioning in the same language, examination of the same language, I understand his position but I think I would like him to understand our position. If we have to make notes -- if we have to take notes, if we have to write down what happened and spend time in doing that, even if it is just doesn't seem a lot of time, that would imply for the Defence the waste of -- losing concentration regarding the transcript and losing the topic itself. You know that this is -- I am the only one who is doing this particular task here on the Defence Bench, and if I don't do it immediately, I will lose my concentration of what is happening at the time that it is happening. So I don't think that this solution is acceptable, either, which I regret, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is very much concerned about both the aspects: First, the interruption of the testimony of the witness but, of course, also on the language problems. Let me first make clear that the Chamber admires the work done by the interpreters. Nevertheless, it is a task I would not easily perform. And that means that if you have to translate for a long period of time, it is unavoidable that now and then, especially when we are talking about all kind of very technical details and put in sometimes a very specific meaning in words, that now and then there might be some translations that could be subject of remarks in respect of whether this is exactly the translation of what the speaker intended to say. So it has got nothing to do with criticism to the interpreters. We admire your job but, nevertheless, this is part of the reality of life. After having said this, if for the understanding of the question it is necessary to interfere with the translation of that question, it can be done when the question has been put to the witness. If there is any other matter which is really urgent which would not allow to wait until the end of the day, the observation can be made after the witness has responded to the question. But this should be the exception. Even if it is sometimes a nuisance that we have to write down things and that we lose concentration, it nevertheless should be done unless it is really of such an urgency that we cannot wait until the end of the day, and then it should be done after the witness has answered the question. So if it is about the translation of the question, it can be done immediately. If it is really, really urgent, but not in relation to the translation of the question itself, it can be done after the witness has answered the question, and all other observations should be made by the end of the day. You have your own lists. So you inform me then, well, let us say five minutes before we stop, and say, "page so and so, line so and so, translation was this; should be in my view, that." This is the ruling and that -- yes. Then, Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. President. I call General Sir Michael Rose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the meantime, Mr. President, does this mean that we will have to stop 10 minutes before the end of the session in order to wash the transcript, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends on how long your list is. If you just have one remark, it can be done in one minute. If you have written down 12 observations, perhaps you can do it in six or seven minutes. Just ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Rose, I presume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Ierace, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, is your nationality English?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It is, but it is described as British.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not to do with the transcript for once, this is a translation -- this is a rule, I think, whether a witness is testifying with or without notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is nothing on his desk, so there was no reason at this moment to interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are notes before the witness. That is the reason why I am intervening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General, before you would consult any notes or any writings, would you please indicate that you need to do so and then we will decide whether we will permit you to do so. Because your testimony, well, should be first from your memory. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, during your military career, did you have active service in various regions, including the Middle East and the Falkland Islands?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you knighted in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On the 5th of January, 1994, were you appointed the commander of the United Nations Protection Force in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you take up that position on the 23 of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were your headquarters based in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was your predecessor in that position Lieutenant General Briquemont?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who were your chiefs -- I'll withdraw that. Did you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. But to facilitate the task of the Prosecution, I think Defence is allowing leading questions. But if we are going this fast, then we are going to have transcript problems. I think that the Prosecution should bear this in mind as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace. The speed is such that both transcript and translation might have some problems. Would you please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you hold that position until the 23 of January, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who were your chiefs of staff in that period?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The initial one was Brigadier, or Colonel at the time, Gordon, I think, and the next one was Van Baal, who was there for most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was the head of Sector Sarajevo, Brigadier General Soubirou?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, having arrived in Sarajevo, did you set about having meetings with the relevant political and military heads of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you first meet with the relevant heads on the Serb side on the 30th of January?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: As far as my memory serves me, that is the date I met them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Whereabouts did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think there were two meetings: One was in Pale with Karadzic and Koljevic and Krajisnik, I think, and the next one was with Mladic, General Mladic, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you accompanied by anyone at those two meetings on that day?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I would have been accompanied by the military assistant Colonel Shadbolt and the interpreter, Captain Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you also from time to time during meetings meet with these people in the company of Viktor Andreev?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: He usually accompanied us as the United Nations authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was he a UN civil advisor?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you also sometimes accompanied by Sergio De Mello?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes, Sergio De Mello was responsible for Sarajevo and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And was he the UN head of Civil Affairs at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, at that first meeting with Dr. Karadzic and later General Mladic, what issues, if any, did you discuss in relation to the part of the conflict in Sarajevo, if any?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: We would have been discussing the need for the ceasefire and the demilitarisation of the area, and also the need to sustain the flow of aid through to the people who needed it, who, of course, were not only the Bosnian Muslim, but also the Croats and the Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were there any particular aspects of the armed conflict in Sarajevo that caused you particular concern?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The whole city had been reduced to a state of siege and, of course, the ambitions of the United Nations were to ensure that the shelling and the sniping and shooting in and around Sarajevo was halted and that the -- there was freedom of movement in and out of that city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did that shelling and sniping impact at all on the civilian population in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Inevitably.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was that a topic that you ever raised with General Mladic or Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I am listening to the French channel. They really have difficulties in their --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will slow down, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was that you first raised that issue, that is, the shelling and sniping of civilians in Sarajevo, with the Serb political and military leadership?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I guess it would have been on the 30th of January, the day we first met them, because it was the prevailing problem facing the United Nations and the people of Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You said that you raised that issue frequently with those individuals. What were the range of responses that, firstly, General Mladic gave to your complaints?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, the general reply was that they were responding to attacks by the Bosnian Muslim army and that that was their method of responding. They didn't have the same level of infantry available to them. The Bosnian army were continually attacking across the line of contact, and their response was shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In your protest to them on that topic, did you make clear that your concern was deliberate or indiscriminate targeting of civilians by shelling and sniping?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: We certainly raised the targeting of civilians as the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. You are listening, like I am, the French booth. But the previous answer of the witness has not been normally interpreted, that is the fact that the Bosniak army continued its attacks across the contact lines. It is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could perhaps repeat your last question and could the witness repeat his answer. That would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I think that if the witness could just speak a little more slowly, it will be easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...look at the screen in front of you and as soon as the cursor stops moving, that means that everyone has been able to translate or to prepare the transcript. And only then answer the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object to the question, but I have to say that the speed with which the questions are being asked, and if I am continuing to do this task of a scribe, I am going to have to intervene. I apologise, General. But the question asked Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by Mr. Ierace, implying that there was a voluntary element, that is a deliberate element, while this witness didn't even indicate this, seems to me that it is an unacceptable question since it contains leading elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will be happy to withdraw the question and rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very happy to have Mr. Ierace do this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think it is enough when I permitted Mr. Ierace to rephrase the question and there is no need for any further comment to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, you told us that you arrived in Sarajevo on the 23rd of January and that it is consistent with your recollection that your first meeting took place on the 30th of January. In that first week, did you form any view as to whether or not civilians in Sarajevo were being deliberately or indiscriminately targeted by -- in the form of shelling and sniping, by forces on the Serb military side of the confrontation line? And please wait a minute before you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Ierace should clarify his question, make it more specific. We know that in Sarajevo there were areas, that is Serb areas, that were shelled by some sides. Could Mr. Ierace -- does Mr. Ierace mean that that would be all sides in Sarajevo that -- including the Serbs that were shelled by the Muslims in an indiscriminate way or does Mr. Ierace also include other parts of the town, and could he say which ones, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, this took you five lines to make this comment. You could have said: "Does the question relate to the whole territory of Sarajevo or certain parts of it?" That is one line and it would be perfectly enough. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, would you mind perhaps re-reading that question on the transcript in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It was certainly the general view of the time and I was only briefed on those lines that there was indiscriminate shelling of civilians and a number of -- by the Serbs and a number of incidents which occurred immediately prior to my arrival and shortly afterwards supported that view. But it is also the case that of course shelling was going the other way from time to time as well against the Serbs in places like Grbavica and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the scale of shelling in Sarajevo in that first week, in that first period when you arrived, in terms of approximate number of shells that were impacting in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It used to be as high as 1500, 2.000 shells a day in Sarajevo which, of course, meant going both ways, not just one way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What about the sniping? In general terms, what was the level of sniping? And perhaps you could respond to this question in terms of how often would you hear the sound of small-arms fire and run the risk of being sniped in that first period?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It was prevalent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Coming back to the question I asked you about five minutes ago, when you raised this issue with General Mladic, did you make clear that your concern was the deliberate or indiscriminate targeting of civilians, quite separate from unavoidable civilian casualties as part of legitimate armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Certainly, we would have raised that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, the answer or the response that you have told us you received frequently, and I think it was that it was justified by him on the basis of they were responding to attacks by the Bosnian government forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is a permissible leading question, in my respectful submission, because I invited the witness to confirm that that was evidence he gave a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will re-read the question, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, the answer or the response you told us that you received frequently, and I think it was, "It was justified by him, on the basis of they were responding to attacks by the government forces." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you form any view in your mind as to whether that was an acceptable justification?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It was very difficult to say at that time, shortly after my arrival, whether that was justifiable or not. Certainly, there was subsequent evidence that Bosnian government forces would deliberately place their firing positions in areas such as the Kosevo hospital in order to attract responses from the Bosnian Serb army in that area. But that was later on. At that time, the week of my arrival, it was a very confused situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On the 4th of February, which I think would be within the first fortnight of your arrival, was there an incident involving a series of mortar explosions in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, there was people forming up to collect United Nations rations. I think it was in the afternoon. And four mortar shells fell in this crowd and a number of people were killed and injured. I think six or ten people were killed and about 28 injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were any steps taken to examine the crater impact sites and ascertain, if possible, the direct and source of fire of those four mortar shells that you remember?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Certainly, crater analysis was performed almost immediately and the evidence from that, of course, one can't be certain in these situations. It is a very inexact science. The evidence pointed quite clearly that it had been the Bosnian Serb army who had fired these shells and clearly targeted the civilians queuing up for these rations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The following day, was there -- before I go on to the following day, what steps, if any --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel and the witness please make pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have to take notes as you have asked me, I will never be able to do this, because I think the Prosecution is trying even to accelerate. I don't think that this is normal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What steps, if any, did you take by way of a protest following your receipt of the results of the crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: My memory says that we would certainly have sent a message of protest and demand of an explanation to the headquarters in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does your memory serve your sufficiently to indicate whether you ever received a reply to that protest?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving a specific reply to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was there another incident the following day?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There was the incident in the marketplace where a similar group of civilians, this time in the market, were targeted by somebody who fired a single mortar bomb on this occasion, and I think 50 plus people were killed and a hundred or more injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you take steps in relation to that incident to carry out a technical examination of the mortar impact site?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: We did. And there definitely was one mortar bomb falling. It is difficult to work out the direction from which it came and also with any accuracy, and also the distance. And so there was a general analysis done, but it was impossible to say precisely from where that mortar bomb had been fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was the investigation, as you recollect it, able nevertheless to establish a direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think it came from the north-east, if I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And when you say that it was impossible to say precisely from where that mortar bomb had been fired, is it the position that having established the direction and having observed that the direction traversed the confrontation lines, that the source of fire may have been on either side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Who established the -- who set the terms of reference for the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There were two investigations, an immediate one which would have been established by Sector Sarajevo, General Soubirou, and there was a subsequent one because of the importance and significance of this very major attack. That was ordered, I think, by Zagreb, and an independent team came and did an analysis. But both came up with the same conclusion, that it was impossible to say from where this bomb had been fired. Indeed, there was a theory that it had been dropped by hand from a nearby building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have to go back to the previous question. I really apologise because I am doing this belatedly, but this has to do with a question which is mentioning the fact that the mortar would have crossed the confrontation lines, and I am afraid that question was a leading question because the witness had not before brought in these elements into his answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, indeed, it was a leading question, and I would have thought the considerable body of evidence as to the results of that report, that that was hardly a controversial issue as to what the report said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I should add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we look at what we know about confrontation lines that were, I would say around the city, or is this in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is not in dispute, then the question might be not very useful, because whatever direction you choose, the direction always crosses a confrontation line. If you take a circle and you take one point from within that circle, whatever direction you chose, it will always cross the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The problem is, Mr. President, is that we have here a plural, the confrontation "lines," and this confrontation lines would mean that if we had crossed several lines, that means that we have crossed the Serb and the Muslim lines and, therefore, that can only mean one thing, that this had gone from the Serb side. It is an "S" as in plural and that gives a determining sense meaning to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking about the direction. If you do not know any distance, we have the previous answer of the witness, that you say if you can't establish the distance, then a direction as such, which is an arrow, will always cross a line if it is within a circle, and whether that a double line or a single line or whether it is from inside or outside the circle is not answered by that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I might be able to help. Probably a single time the confrontation line because, of course, you have two sides --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was part of the question and not of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that the thing wasn't very clear in the French transcript, and this is what happens in problems with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, you were saying that there were two investigations, General Soubirou had ordered the first, and the terms of reference or, rather, the -- General Soubirou had ordered the first and given the importance and significance of this very major attack, to use your words, Zagreb ordered a second one which was carried out by an independent team that came from outside and did an analysis. You said that both investigations arrived at the same conclusion. You said that there was an idea that it had been dropped by hand from a nearby building. Did that theory find favour with either of the two investigations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the nature of the investigations, tell us something of the terms of reference to this extent: Did they go beyond a technical examination of the crater impact site?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were they the only investigations carried out by the UN, the one ordered by General Soubirou, and then the second one where the terms -- the second one that was ordered from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you tell us something about indeed the impact that this incident had on perhaps the whole war, but certainly, the war in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It created an opportunity for progress towards peace, and the people were so horrified by what had happened, there was a major initiative launched to bring a halt to the fighting, which certainly proved successful as far as Sarajevo was concerned in that both sides on the 9th, 10th of February agreed to halt the fighting in and around Sarajevo, to withdraw their heavy weapons and to open up certain routes for civilian aid convoys. And that transformed the whole of the situation in Bosnia which, up to then, had been one of decline and deterioration. And this was the first hope people had of peace and, indeed, Sarajevo started to slowly return to normality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you tell us something in which the way that manifested the return to normality in that initial post-Markale period? How did it impact, for instance, on the daily lives of the civilians of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It was possible to repair the electricity lines, the water supply was restored in many areas. Civil aid convoys and, indeed, commercial convoys were run in and out of Sarajevo and there was some movement of civilians across the line of conflict as well. Indeed, there was a weekly bus that ran to Zenica from Sarajevo across the battle line so that the people can go and visit their relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The former Markale, if I can refer to it that way, would one see civilians, day or night, wandering the streets at a walking pace, sitting at cafes outside, doing that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The danger of shelling and sniping was too great.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And after Markale?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: After Markale, that started to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What about the trams in that immediately period before Markale, were they running?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: They were not running but, again, with the restoration of the electricity supply and the halting of fighting in and around Sarajevo, it was possible to restore the tram service in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again in that initial period, having regard to your last few answers, was it the case that the sniping, firstly, had almost completely fallen away in those first few days?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No. Nothing ends immediately in a confused civil war situation, but certainly the sniping died down to a very low level indeed, although there was always the odd shot being taken --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last question? We lost him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But it was not a thing which had sufficient effect to stop the slow restoration of normality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What about the shelling --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could the witness please repeat the last question? The French booth apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General, I thought you would have heard it, the request by the interpreters. I don't know what channel you are listening to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would take channel 4, which is the English channel, that means that there is no translation at all, you would have heard that the interpreters asked you to repeat the -- I take it the last answer. That was the answer starting with: "Nothing ends immediately in a confused civil war situation but certainly the sniping died down to a very low level indeed, although there was always the odd shot --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Being taken. It was not at a sufficient level to prevent the slow return to normality which started to occur at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Ierace, the next question was about the shelling and that is where the interpreters intervened. So could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What observations would you make in terms of pre-Markale and post-Markale in respect of shelling?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It halted completely. The agreement that was arrived at required the withdrawal of all heavy weapons from a 20 kilometre [Realtime transcript read in error "millimetre"] circle around Sarajevo centre, which I think was the Bridge of Friendship and Peace that crossed the river between Grbavica and the main part of the city. And the Bosnian government forces were required to withdraw all their heavy weapons into the barracks within the city and not use them. And that more or less was achieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that is millimetres, kilometre. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an important information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the fact that the sniping, to a large extent, and the shelling entirely cease following the decisions made by the military commanders in the wake of Markale suggest anything to you as to the degree of command and control that the military leadership on all sides of the warring factions exercised?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes, it showed that there was an absolute --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. If I have to intervene after the questions, like you said, then really we need to have time. The French booth, I don't think, interpreted. The question was also related to sniping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that is a matter of translation. You could have --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it is an error on my part. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...at the end of the day. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace. Would you please be more careful, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it seems that as a result of Mr. Piletta-Zanin's objection, that the interpreters were not able to complete the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, if you need refresh your memory as to the question, perhaps you could read it on the screen. You will see that your answer was not completely recorded. Would you mind please repeating your answer?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes. The halting of the shelling and the almost but total halting of the sniping at that time showed that there was a total and absolute control on both sides of the military machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, as part of this new preparedness to cooperate with the UN, were there some access routes established which became known as "blue routes"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the "blue routes" were? What was the nature of a blue route?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The nature of a blue route is that these were routes which the UN aid convoys could use, without hindrance, to deliver aid in and out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, over the ensuing weeks, what happened in terms of progress in Sarajevo, that is in relation to the part of the conflict that took place in Sarajevo and perhaps in terms of regression?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Well, there was a general improvement in the security situation in and around Sarajevo which lasted until mid-September, when the Bosnian government forces broke the ceasefire in a very major way, hence started to decline again. Now, up to then, there had been issues from time to time where incidents had occurred, sniping incidents, and that had all been raised and an effort was made to bring about an anti-sniping treaty or agreement. But that would seem to be always requiring trade-offs in some other area and was very hard to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to the anti-sniping agreement, was that signed eventually on the 14th of August, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That sounds about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I presume the Defence has no objection to leading as to the terms of the anti-sniping agreement. I imagine that is common ground. Did the anti-sniping agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have interpretation, Mr. President. I do not -- I did not hear Mr. Ierace's question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether there was an objection to the contents of the anti-sniping project.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Ierace be more specific as to which project of agreement? Could he perhaps tell us which agreement is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you read the English Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. transcript, you would see that it is the agreement of the 14th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is the one signed by Mr. Milovanovic, then there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, I am very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did that agreement require the warring factions to cease sniping activities against military personnel, civilians, and UN personnel in the region of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, over what period of time did those negotiations leading up to the signing of the agreement, take place, and just approximately?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: A matter of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And who did you deal with on the Serb army side in those negotiations, both yourself and your immediate subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The general relationship between the UN headquarters in Sarajevo and the Bosnian Serb army was the highest level achieved between me and General Mladic, who was supported by his aide, Tolimir - Colonel Tolimir, I think he was at the time - and also the Chief of Staff, Milovanovic, General Milovanovic. There were other people who would -- and obviously, General Galic had a part to play, although he did not seem to me to have the overriding ability for decision making. That was always held higher up the chain of command. So the main negotiations were usually, in terms of Bosnia-wide and sometimes in terms of Sarajevo, decision making was achieved between General Mladic and me. Although sometimes the documents were signed by the people, General Gvero, who was another one who was involved on the Bosnian Serb army side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you form any views to whether the bare fact that the side --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I apologise. I have to intervene. A whole sentence has not been interpreted in the French transcript. I have to say from "General Gvero who was involved on the Bosnian Serb army side," this has not been interpreted and I think the French booth will agree with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will change to the French channel again to keep a closer eye on what happens. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, did you form any view as to whether the bare fact that the parties at a senior military level were negotiating the terms of the cessation of sniping against civilians indicated anything to their belief as to their ability to control the sniping, in other words, to turn it off?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes, they had the ability to turn it off for certain. But equally, they were not the principles themselves. It was the politicians who very often took part in what were basically military discussions, but nevertheless there was always a political aspect. And, therefore, you would have some like Krajisnik who would be present at these discussions on the one side, or Muratovic on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now what about the other part played by what one might call "paramilitaries," and in particular on the side of the confrontation lines that were controlled by the Bosnian Serb army? Were there any -- firstly, in your view, were there such forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And in your view, was there ever any demonstrated ability on the part of the regular Bosnian Serb army to control the paramilitary when they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes. There was a group of people, mercenaries, we thought, that were positioned on the Jewish cemetery on the Bosnian Serb side and who did not seem to accept the terms of the agreement to halt the shelling and sniping in and around Sarajevo. And after some effort had been made by the UN, the Bosnian Serbs finally brought into Sarajevo, into Grbavica, an element which we thought were probably regular Yugoslav troops to go and deal with these people, which they duly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And, therefore, was the Jewish cemetery a source of fire during your period in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It always remained a dangerous place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say though that they duly did, what did they actually do and what did they achieve by their action?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think they re-established a chain of command which maybe had been weakened by the existence of these mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Approximately when was that action by the army forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I guess about a month after the agreement had been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is the anti-sniping agreement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No, the original agreement in the 9th or 10th of February.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: 1994. So maybe March they would have dealt with these mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Again in terms of highlights in terms of progress, was there some progress with the Grbavica bridge?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes. It was possible to open up the bridge and to move certainly personnel across, civilian as well as military, the UN military, that is. And also some supplies moved over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recall the month that the bridge was reopened?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think it must have been in February of 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down in the questions and the answers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that the interpreters have even no time to take a breath, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is fourth or fifth time that this problem is -- but I cannot take notes. I cannot take notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace should slow down, and when he does - I asked him several times - there is no further use to explain that it is difficult for you as well. The Chamber understands.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You told us earlier that the trams were not running before Markale. At some stage after Markale, did they recommence operating?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again, do you recall approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It would have taken about a month to restore electricity and to repair the trams and get them going again, so maybe by April they were running.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the trams have any particular symbolic significance, in your view, to the view that the civilians of Sarajevo themselves would have in terms of hope for ultimate peace?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think that the restoration of the tram service gave the people of Sarajevo hope that peace would be restored and that they could live normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, on the other side of the coin, so as to speak, during the time that you were in Sarajevo, were there any incidents that came to your attention in terms of reports, investigations conducted by the UN, which suggested that forces on the side of the confrontation lines controlled by Bosnian government forces had deliberately targeted civilians within the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There was certainly some suspicion, but before I arrived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to ask you to wait until the cursor stops moving.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was certainly some suspicion before I arrived in Sarajevo that -- and allegations had appeared in the media, and there was certainly suspicions that that was happening after I arrived. What was certain is that the Bosnian government forces would, from time to time, fire at the Serbs, at particular moments of political importance, in order to draw back fire on to Sarajevo so that the Bosnian government could demonstrate the continuing plight of the people in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think in that regard you mentioned Kosevo hospital?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Certainly they were firing, a Bosnian -- neither side totally respected the withdrawal of heavy weapons and hid some within that 20 kilometre circle. The Bosnian government forces had, I think, three tanks and some other heavy weapons which they kept hidden in a tunnel and that would -- they would bring these out from time to time, particularly after the breakdown of the ceasefire in September, and fire at the Bosnian Serbs in order to attract fire back. And usually, they positioned their tanks or mortars in and around sensitive areas, such as close to the UN headquarters in by the hospital, by a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were steps taken on those occasions to complain to the appropriate political authorities and military authorities on the Bosnian government side?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: All the time protests were made, mainly to Mr. Ganic, who seemed to head up the military operations on the Bosnian government side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to sniping, did you ever have occasion to see any of the sniping weaponry that was deployed by either side in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Certainly I saw on one occasion a Bosnian government sniper who was a young boy carrying, I think, a Simonov rifle with a telescopic sight close to the Bridge of Friendship and Peace, coming out of a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is Simonov spelled S-i-m-o-n-o-v?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think so. Both sides were sniping at each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that completes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Is the Defence -- no, I think we first then should have the break because you were asking us a decision on the -- on the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On one hand, Mr. President. On the other hand, bearing in mind of the new case law of your Chamber and the time that I needed to jot down remarks, we needed to confer with General Galic, therefore, we are now not ready to proceed with the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest then that we have an early break for half an hour, and Mr. Ierace, you wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just rise to my feet to observe that we have made excellent progress in examination-in-chief. There isn't another witness to called today so if Mr. Piletta-Zanin wants more time and it suits the Trial Chamber, there would be no objection from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. How much time would you need, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask this question. Just a moment. We will need time until 11.00, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the examination-in-chief took 55 minutes, if we would start at 11.00, that would mean that the Defence can be expected to conclude its cross-examination before the next break then; that is at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What will be the time of the next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we start again at 11.00, that would be at 12.30. Yes. Then we will adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence has asked that the Chamber would give a decision on what is called the "grattage." It is about the document P3061 tendered by the Prosecution. That document consists of two parts. The first part is a series of post-mortems and the second part is a list of 50 patients that have been evacuated on the 6th of February and, well, let me say the pages 00268597 up to last three digits 603. That is the second part of the document. The Chamber is not satisfied by the explanation as it has been given until now in the reports of the Prosecutor on the, I would say, double entries. Especially the date, the 5th of February, 1994, seems to be a second entry at that same place very often in different position and in different intensity of typewriting. Therefore, since the explanation has not been satisfying until now, these documents are not admitted into evidence. At the same time, the Chamber wonders whether the parties would agree on aspects of this incident, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I have some difficulties in looking at you because there is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is also true for my side. I am sorry about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it is not your fault. But the Chamber wonders whether the parties disagree, first of all, on the fact that a shell did fall on the marketplace on the day, the 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, if this is a question, I think I can answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will just see what -- in what -- what is in dispute between the parties and what is not. So my question is about whether a shell fell on the market, on the Markale market, on the 5th of February and exploded. That is the first question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can give you an immediate answer. The Defence has already said in some of the questions -- in some of the questions that we asked, that it was equally possible that a manufactured bomb, a shell, was voluntarily positioned in the market previously and in some way that there was a kind of scenario that was put into place. On the other hand, we cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could not agree on whether there was anything that fell on the market. Would the parties agree that there was an explosion on the market on the 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have to confer. I think, in fact, that since there was an explosion, I don't think that we can reasonably contest this. I am trying to look at my colleague and the General. Yes, I think that they are nodding their heads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next question would be whether the parties could agree on, let's say, 50-plus people killed by this explosion?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Mr. President. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which -- could you say whether it is the position of the Defence that people were killed by this explosion, but less than 50, or was there no one killed by this explosion?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. The Defence, and particularly General Galic, were not concerned by this incident, but the position of the Defence consists of saying that here I must make a parallel with Timisoara, which is a very well-known incident in the manipulation of the media, when we don't know whether the dead died on the marketplace and, therefore, is it 50 plus, less than 50, and so on. It is up to the Prosecution to prove this, not the contrary

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...of course. But I am just trying to find out what is in dispute between the parties. Is it the position of the Defence that no one was killed on the market by this explosion?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you are placing Defence in a very uncomfortable position. Imagine if there was a -- let's say that there was an explosion and there was a set-up, and perhaps there may have been three people who died. Imagine that the rest is comparable to the Timisoara affair. How could I give you an answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your answer is clear, that you do not exclude that, and that is the position of the Defence, that no one was killed by this explosion?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is negatively presented. I think that seems better, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that is at least clear. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, two points. There has been --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace started telling us something and I would like to have him continue. No, no, no, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Two points, Mr. President. Firstly, the Prosecution has called already witnesses who gave evidence that, immediately after the explosion, they observed countless people dead and wounded. It has not been put to those witnesses that they were lying or otherwise mistake. Secondly, a minor point, my friend refers to a well-known incident in the media which I think he said was Timisoara. Perhaps he could spell that for the benefit of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please do so, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I am just reading the transcript. That is Timisoara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked to spell it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will spell it in French. That is T-i-m-i-s-o-a-r-a. Timisoara is located, I can tell Mr. Ierace, on the Danube river, more or less south of Romania, close to Hungary. Both countries are in Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is our ruling on the admission into evidence of these documents. Let me just one moment confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that, the last question in this respect, that the Defence also take as similar position in respect of wounded people as a result of this explosion?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that goes without saying, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then are you ready to cross-examine General Rose?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but just to give additional clarification, be more specific, this can happen -- this witness is a crucial witness. He gave a statement of about 20 pages. It may happen that we have to go over the limit. We are hesitating, Mr. President, that we were hesitating as to calling this witness as to one of our witnesses, but out of courtesy for Sir Michael Rose, if we can go a little bit over the limit so that we don't have to get him to come back like some other witnesses. I think that will be a gain for justice in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no doubt, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that you have to conclude the cross-examination by today. We will consider whether you could continue after the next break, but there is no question about taking more than today, let me be clear. And we start with the point that it Defence gets as much time as the Prosecution took. And it will very much depend also on the way you cross-examine the witness whether extra time will be allowed. Just to give you some guidance, if you thank the witness for each Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and every answer he gives, that takes under cross-examination altogether five minutes. If you ask, as you did with the last witness, four or five questions whether he was a man with good training and then without any follow-up in other questions, we take it that if the General is in front of us, that even without asking him five questions on whether he considers himself to be a good, well-educated military man and therefore he will have a good assessment of a lot of situations, that usually is only relevant if some doubt comes up as to the competence of this person. I just note that yesterday, I think you put four or five questions in that respect without any follow-up, and if you use your time in that way, then, of course, the Chamber might be more hesitant to grant extra time. Could Madam Usher please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But, of course, we believe that we can do it in less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's see what happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Rose, you will now be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. Thank you for being here. I know you speak French very well.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Not perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will ask questions in French. General, would you like me to call you Sir Michael or General? What do you prefer?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It is whatever pleases you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will call you "Sir" or "General."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It is your --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, I would like you to confirm to me that you gave a written witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 24th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, by courtesy, I appreciate that you are looking at me, but I think that the Chamber also needs to hear your answer. Now, General, to make things simple, and with the leave of the Chamber, I will hand your statement of the 24th of May, 1995, so that you can confirm your -- identify your signature, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This statement, Mr. President, has also been giving to the booth, the interpretation booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will it be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't know that yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. That is the document that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, General, to gain time, we are going to look at this document together, and I would be very grateful if you could go to directly to page two of the witness statement, please, and to go to the end of the penultimate paragraph on this page. I will read what you stated here. And in advance, I thank you for your indulgence with my accent. You said the following [In English]: "Is included to Bosnian Serbs looking for a global ceasefire starting with the demilitarisations of Sarajevo." First question, General, is it true that at this particular point --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that at this particular point, the forces as those commanded by General Galic wished not to have war but, on the contrary, to have global ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And, General, if you let me, I will continue. And a ceasefire starting with the demilitarisation of Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is appropriate for the witness to be allowed to complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You interrupted him. Did you answer the question as you wished to do? Or would you like to add something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could add that the Bosnian Serb army were in the military ascendancy and that it was in their interest to halt the fighting at that moment, politically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: However, the question I was asking before I was being interrupted, General, is this one: Is it true - if you can answer by a "yes" or a "no", please - that at that particular point the Serb army that is commanded by General Galic did not wish war, but peace?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] For your answer. Thank you very much for that. [Interpretation], General, I would like us now to go to a following question, General. You spoke a great deal earlier about an attack on Markale. I used the term "attack" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you change to that, I have some difficulties in understanding your answer to the question. The question was whether it was true that at a particular point the Serb army that is commanded by General Galic did not wish war, but peace. And then you said -- the answer is translated in the transcript; I think you answered in French. You said: "Yes, on the contrary," which sounds a bit contradictory, as a matter of fact. You can say "yes" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Am I permitted to clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time, the Serbs, and we are talking about Sarajevo only because elsewhere there was a civil war going on, at that point, it was in the political interest for the Serb army to have peace in and around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I still do not understand then what "on the contrary" means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the contrary, they were not pursuing at that point a war policy in and around Sarajevo. They had agreed to a peaceful withdrawal of their heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, just to be clear on this point, is it true that at that particular point the Serb forces wanted more than that, they wanted a demilitarisation, total demilitarisation, of the zone of Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It was one of their stated aims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, so it is true to say, according to what you know, that at that point - I am not talking about the war, I am talking about the events - there was a military and political will on the Serb side, was not just to withdraw weapons but obliteration in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, I would like to come back to the point of Markale. I am just going to go superficially in relation to what I call "an attack." Yes, an attack, in French an "attentat" is an attack in English when it doesn't concern --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry, the interpreters' booth would like to intervene for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. But I just have to underline this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Not a shelling. Is it true, General, that you said that such events were susceptible to happen chronologically, at certain periods of time when, elsewhere on the international scene, there were important events which were about to happen? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think that I said that the event had international significance which allowed political progress to be made. It was the event which had the effect on the international community, not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Indeed. General, didn't you say publicly, on some occasions, that what happened in this type of civil wars in Sarajevo, that some events comparable to Markale occurred chronologically just at a given point in time when we are waiting for certain -- anticipating some decisions on the international scene? For instance, to be more precise, at a given time when we are expecting or hoping for military interventions from the outside, for instance, NATO intervention?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Certainly, there have been occasions when military events were used to produce international responses favourable to one side or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, General. Do you think -- do you think that such events could have been provoked with this purpose in mind, with this objective in mind, in order to get some political gain?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Let us go back to Markale and what followed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you change from subject, I would like you -- I let you finish and let the witness finish the answer because we have a nonaudible response on page 44, line 21. You were asked, General, whether there was a military and political will on the Serb side not just to withdraw weapons but obliteration in and around Sarajevo, and I think your answer was in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could not be understood by the interpreter. It has been clarified. May I ask the interpreters' booth, I see on page 45, line 1, that the interpreter would like to intervene. Is the problem solved or is the problem not solved?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter booth notes that the word French "attentat" in the case of incident would have to be interpreted as "attack," not as assassination attempt. JUDGE ORIE That has been clarified then as well. Mr. Ierace, is there --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There is another "no audible response" at page 46, line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is where you were asked whether such events could have been provoked with such a purpose in mind, with this objective in mind, in order to get some political gain. I think your answer was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's possible, yes. Could you please, especially if these answers are very short, first wait until the cursor stops moving and then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, before thanking the witness for his answer, could you please pause as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
