utterances.text: Sir, if we can continue and go back to Markale. Is it true that even after the incident of Markale, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, who was in charge in command of the Muslim forces, was still not -- did not agree with the demilitarisation of Sarajevo? [In English] You say that is true?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. General, I would now like to focus my attention on the period of February 1994 and the beginning of 1994. I would like you to go to page 5 of your own statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, you said the following, and I am going to quote you now: [In English] "Serbs were favourable to the suggestion of a global ceasefire." [Interpretation] Are we still in this period of 1994? It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it may be that the answer will clarify this, but in case it doesn't, this question began with the observation by my friend that he was focussing the witness's attention on the periods of February 1994 and the beginning of 1994. Having said that, he went straight to this quote. It is apparent from a entry in the preceding sentence that it relates to April 1994. So in order to avoid confusion, I think that should be made clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I precisely wanted to ask the question to the General, find out whether his affirmation would have covered the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the ceasefire around Sarajevo, the United Nations proceeded with their efforts to turn what was a local ceasefire into a more global cessation of hostilities, and during that time we received the assistance of Mr. Redman, United States foreign service, and this comment came from discussions we had after February, in April, discussing a global cessation of hostilities. At that time, the Serbs were in favour of a general global cessation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, I would like to ask you which would be simpler for you, if you have good glasses, to read the last paragraph of that page, beginning with [In English] "They told me that they ..." et cetera. [Interpretation] Would you please do it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are following my line on a global ceasefire, they said they were now prepared to enter talks on a ceasefire based on the plan proposed by Viktor Andreev and myself, and on the plan being borne by the Geneva Peace Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, would you agree with me -- thank you for much for the French booth who has been running, trying to catch up with me. Would you agree that there was a very significant evolution in regard to the position of Serb militaries and politicians in that period who were trying to seek peace?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the passage that the witness was invited to read was not, in fact, the paragraph but rather it commenced at the third sentence in the paragraph. The first two sentences clarified who "they" were, and in order that Your Honours can follow the full sense of the quote, it would be appropriate surely for my friend to bring out who "they" were. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just to gain time, since we have been provided with the text, the line before reads: "Then I saw Dr. Karadzic and Mladic. So "they" is sufficiently explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I thought that it was clear that we were referring to Serb politicians and military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will add to my reply something that I have already said, that at this point, the Serbs controlled much of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 70 per cent, and it was in their interest at that point to declare a ceasefire and pursue some political settlement, as they had the military advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for your answer. General, is it true that the Serbs in that period, and I would ask you to answer by a "yes" or "no," wished a ceasefire, a global ceasefire for a period of at least one year?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true, consequently -- is it true, consequently, that the opposed forces did not want to -- if speaking about the ceasefire, would want this for a limited period of time, four weeks, perhaps four months?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...four months, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that the political aim sought by the Sarajevo forces which we refer to as Presidency was to gain time in order to organise military construction and to begin fighting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It's certainly possible that that is what they were hoping to achieve, but, of course, I am not able to make a precise analysis of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speaking to you as -- since you are a General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, page 50, line 12, and I think that problem at that point arises from the need for my learned colleague and the witness to pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think the answer is clear. It was four months. And I think an intervention of this kind is wasting our time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am quite sure that the answer was longer than "four months," that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please make pauses? And I had some difficulties in following the weeks and the months as well, although, finally, I understood that these were months and not weeks. You showed some irritation before, and so did Mr. Ierace, on the interruptions. Would you please all refrain from expressing your irritation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very gladly, Mr. President. I will be -- I will adopt a British flavour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, is it true, General, in order to clarify this matter, that consequently it was possible that the Bosniak side of the Sarajevo side tried to gain time to reconstruct its military operations --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...explained, the Bosnian government saw their position as being one of a victim state subject to aggression. They had the moral right, in their view, to recover their lost territories. So the logic that you propose is entirely possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, in that sense, do you know whether there was an exploitation of the media in that period?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, to the extent that General Galic's Corps was interested in some events --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No audible response. I didn't hear it as well as not being able to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see. The answer was in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It certainly was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "It certainly was" was the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the situation may be assisted if the microphone could be repositioned, given that the General is facing towards Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please even the left microphone, perhaps to be put a bit more in front of the table.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness wait until the end of interpretation, please, before answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the cable is long enough, to go a bit more to the corner of table, to what is for you, the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, before intervening for the same reason, Mr. Ierace, the booth is simply asking you to make a pause before providing the answer. I suppose that is what Mr. Ierace wanted to say. I, personally, can hear your answers perfectly well in English. General, I spoke of Gorazde. Do you know that city?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether in Gorazde there was a huge manipulation in regard to the media?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There was certainly manipulation of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, I will try to summarise this. Is it true, that as far as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I can remember, one simulated on the international plane a situation of attack and crisis which did not extend to that extent in Gorazde at the time? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is not true. There was an attack on Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: To that extent?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...at the start of the attack. Not only by the media but by the government, the Bosnian government as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So do you understand by this is a technique of warfare?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also the record asks to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you answered "yes" to the fact that manipulations of information coming from the Bosnian government was, to your mind, a technique of war?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your very clear answer. Now, I am just checking upon the transcript, not to have any problems in that respect. The response was not audible. I am waiting for the answer to appear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe the answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the witness, it is the recollection -- it is my recollection that the witness said that this was a technique of war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we seem to be having technical problems with the -- capturing the transcript. I think we might have to slow down a little bit. And I am just informing the Chamber of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, do you think that that technique of war, which was the term you used, was employed elsewhere, in Gorazde, for instance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the answer to your question still has to appear before you put a new question to the witness. The answer did not yet appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that it never appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are any specific problems with the transcript, I would like to be informed. I think your answer was in the affirmative, that this technique of war was implied elsewhere, and I think the question was: "Elsewhere and then in Gorazde."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood it to be elsewhere from Sarajevo, for example, in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood the question as being corrected elsewhere from Gorazde, for example, in Sarajevo. Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was the following, Mr. President:

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The technique, General, was it employed in other places, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: To the extent that you have answered yes, has -- was this also used in Sarajevo? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Sir Michael Rose, now I would like to come back to the subject of sniping. Is it exact, is it true, that there were problems in relation to sniping in -- on both sides, on both warring sides?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, when you say, "yes," do you also know - and we think we know it - that it happened that there was firing coming from Muslim marksmen in the direction of -- on their own citizens or on their own persons?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I could never say with any certainty, but there was a suspicion that this may have been the case. Whether that was well-founded or not, impossible to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, you are a man with vast experience, and when you say there was suspicions, those suspicions, were they more than a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think I would be more comfortable with it remaining a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you. General, if you know, was there a sniper unit based near or by the Holiday Inn hotel?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Are you referring to Serb snipers or Bosnian government snipers?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, I am referring to the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...seen one sniper emerging and the French certainly have seen a police team, a sniping team, emerging from buildings close to the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, you are saying that it was a unit because you spoke of a team. Is this the term you used?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, one thing, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, again to make a pause, because the last answer, if you look at your screen, starts with "seen one sniper" and I think it is of major importance, perhaps for the Defence case as well, that it was this witness who told us that he had seen this. Now, since you started your next question too early, or perhaps I must say, General Rose, that you started perhaps your answer too early, that this information which might be very important is missing on the transcript. So I must ask everyone to make that pause in order not to lose evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might that last answer by clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether you should interfere in the cross-examination of the Defence unless there is any specific reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't seek to interfere. It is just that when one looks at the transcript, it is still not clear what General Rose has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would be grateful if I was not interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if Mr. Ierace speaks, you wait until he is finished what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I was just making the point that if one looks at the transcript, for anyone who reads the transcript, it is still not clear what the General said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then please repeat your answer, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have certainly seen one sniper coming out of a building close to the Holiday Inn, and the French reported a paramilitary police team on the Bosnian government side, also coming out of a building in the region of the Holiday Inn. Now, I could add, this was a natural place for the Bosnian government to put snipers if they wished to indulge in counter-snipe activities across the river. Equally, they could be used to confuse the whereabouts of their sniping because of their location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it would seem, this being the case, that we have had difficulties with the transcript today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...aware that this takes time but let's not discuss this in the middle of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, thank you. What I was saying a minute ago, you spoke about a team. Is it true -- is it right to consider that there were units in the technical military sense of the term of "snipers"?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Just to go back to the reply on line 21 of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Rose, I have to interrupt again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think since you did not wait until the cursor stopped moving, the answer to the question, which was "yes," and then you wanted to go back to the reply of line 21. But your answer is now missing from the transcript. So I again have to ask you -- perhaps I do it the following way which we did before, although it may seem a bit childish. With my hand, I give signs who is going to put the next question or who is at that moment going to answer the question. I hate to do it, and I can't do it by speaking because that would even further cause a problem. So if you would please then look to me, both Mr. Piletta-Zanin and you. I am sorry that I have to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that General was about to correct an earlier answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Thank you for your assistance. Would you please tell us what you would like to tell us on line 21? Which now disappeared from your screen. But I could read it for you if you want to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wish to change one word. It should have read "countersniping activities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is in page 57, line 21, it should be: "countersniping." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, is it true that in the book that you devoted to this part of your life, you spoke of, at a certain point, of a firing which took place, a shot that was fired on civilians, near this area, that is what we called the Holiday Inn hotel?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I do not have the book in front of me, but if that is what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you remember that, General? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I certainly have a memory of a suspicion at the time that a Bosnian government sniper team may have fired on one of the trams.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, I am going to take the liberty of reading what you wrote in page 22 of your book called "Fighting for Peace." And you can tell me if this is correct. You were speaking of someone who saw this scene in Sarajevo and you said the following: [In English] Soon after we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The convention has always been that the Defence provides copies of documents from which it reads before it does so. My friend has referred to a page number from --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw this question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, General, if you have written it, then we are going to assume that this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Can you read out what I said?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The question is the following: Could we assume that what you have written in the book is correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question has been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is entirely possible that something I wrote four years ago, five years ago, may subsequently have proved to be inexact. I cannot guarantee that what I wrote in hindsight was always correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Indeed. General, could you confirm, however, that the Bosnian authorities refused to sign initially, in any case, an anti-sniping agreement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There were difficulties, I think, on both sides about the signature, which is why it took so long. I think I explained that both sides wished trade-offs, these political trade-offs, and these are what was causing the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that you said that Mr. Silajdzic and Mr. Ganic were refusing to discuss on any level the cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think it would be more accurate to say that they wished to have certain preconditions met before they would entertain discussion of a cessation of hostilities. This was, of course, in the mid-1994. By the end of 1994, we managed to persuade them to accept a cessation of hostility agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, could you please take the statement that you have before you on page 8 and read the penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That was certainly a true statement for that day. The reason for that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I can hear it well. But could you please read it for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: "On the 23rd of May, I met with Mr. Silajdzic and Mr. Ganic, but both refused to discuss the cessation of hostilities."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, is it then true that at this particular point in time, end of May, 1994, the political authorities, Mr. Silajdzic, and military authorities, Mr. Ganic, were refusing to discuss cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I am now going to continue along the same line. Do you know and could you tell us who is General Delic? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: General Delic was the military commander of all Bosnian government forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that General Delic told you at a certain point that the only possible way for them was the way of total war?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I believe he did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That's what it says in your statement. Thank you for remembering that. General, when your equivalent, General Delic, stated that he had -- there were no other possibilities for them except for total war, this was meant on the level of the entire Bosnia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, that is including Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That appears to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, is it true that Sarajevo was particularly charged with powerful symbolism through its image?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Evidently so, because it was the capital of Bosnia. But, of course, later we managed to interest both General Delic and Mr. Ganic in the idea of a demilitarisation and cessation of hostilities. We achieved the latter, never the former.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Would you agree with me to consider that, militarily speaking or politically speaking, whoever holds Sarajevo holds Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, would you agree with me to consider that the exploitation as the image of Sarajevo as a martyr would be very useful to the cause of the Muslim authorities?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That was evidently the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I would now like to come back more specifically to another interesting point, which is the preparation of maps which were necessary for a peace plan. I would like you to go back to your own statement, and on page 10 of your statement, you can read the very last sentence of the first paragraph, please. [In English] "The UN Civil Affairs."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first paragraph, top of page 10, please, General. The last page -- the last sentence begins with "the UN Civil Affairs."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Would you please read it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: "The UN Civil Affairs believed that the map was deliberately drawn to ensure Bosnian Serb rejection."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you please give us some specification as to the date of this matter of these maps.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General -- yes, I am sorry, we don't have the answer. I perfectly heard "6th of July." It doesn't appear in the transcript. General, could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The date at which the contact group presented the map was the 6th of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In my respectful submission, it is incumbent upon cross-examining counsel to elicit the matter in a coercive means and that requires, in this context, an explanation as to what maps the witness is referring to by reading that line of his statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is perfectly coherent for whoever knows about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you did not respond. You did reprimand, I think - I am not quite sure - the one who asked the question. This Chamber is confronted with one line read about maps, not knowing what it is about. So the observation of Mr. Ierace was totally justified, and if you are asked to respond, I would like you to respond on what has been said and not to reprimand the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do this gladly by asking the following question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, could you please very briefly tell the Chamber and everyone, in fact, what was so important about these maps, what these maps were about?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...group which did not represent necessarily the political views of the United Nations, produced without consultation their own solution to the dividing up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This attempt had been made previously by Mr. Vance, Mr. Owen and others, Stoltenberg included. The Civil Affairs representative in Sarajevo, Mr. Viktor Andreev, considered this map unworkable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you. I would like you to explain what was the contact group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The contact group was a number of countries led by America, including France, Britain, Germany, and others, six nations represented, Russia included. It was an independent attempt to resolve the political -- the problem of the political division of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a European initiative initially to form this group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now, in order to respect the time, could you please tell us how much time we have left? I don't know this because I am going much more slowly than usually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we would have the break at 12.30, and if we would start again at 10 minutes to 1.00, I think that the time -- the Chamber thinks that the time lost by technical problems would be fully compensated if you would continue until a quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, in respect of these questions and matters, now that things are perfectly clear, did you have the impression that on an international level there was a very anti-Serb feeling which made it so -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. resulted in such a way that such a plan could not be immediately accepted?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There was certainly a desire amongst the international community not to reward the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, am I to understand from what you are saying that the international community did not wish to have a plan that would have frozen the positions, perhaps, positions on the ground, and that would have perhaps avoided a lot of suffering?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think that is a fair assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, considering this situation, do you think that the international community perhaps has a relative part of responsibility in this drama that we have to examine today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object to that question, Mr. President. The question bears no relevance to the task that the Trial Chamber faces in determining the issues in this trial. It also involves a reasonably complex consideration of moral issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I ask why this is sustained?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The relevance of issues that we have to examine is for the Chamber to decide and not for a witness. A witness could not tell us what is relevant. You may ask about whatever issue you would like to ask questions, and if there is any objection that it is irrelevant, the Chamber will decide on it. But you cannot ask a witness what are relevant issues to be -- to be examined by this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir Michael, could you testify and tell this Chamber that in the period that we are talking about here, that is the entire 1994, the Serb forces, for whatever reason that may be, they sought, wanted and wished for peace in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That was generally the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, General. Now, I would like us to, in order to finish these questions on snipers, I would like to ask you for a clarification. In relation to this, you mentioned an anti-sniping agreement and also the presence of General Galic. Did you personally see him at these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I really don't remember whether I saw him at these negotiations, personally. I certainly saw him from time to time, but the main level of negotiation and the preparatory were for the anti-sniping agreement, took place between General Galic and Brigadier Soubirou, not between me and General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, it is and may be a surprising question but I am asking it anyway: General Galic who is here presented today, didn't he ever declare to you that he wanted to use snipers in order to kill as many persons as possible in Sarajevo and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Evidently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This concludes the question of the snipers. General, do you know what Tarcin was, briefly?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what Tarcin was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Tarcin, if my memory is correct, was a prison run by the Bosnian government where a number of Serbs were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In which conditions, General?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It was visited once, I think, by the ICRC, and the reports were they were not held in very -- again, my memory tells me were not being held in very good conditions. They were inside a grain silo, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, do you know if there were other prisons in Sarajevo itself where Serb prisoners, detainees, would have been held?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of any prison in Sarajevo where they were -- Serb prisoners were held. Tarcin was outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, I now would like to come back to the reactions that followed the -- immediate follow-up on what was the follow-up of the attack on Markale market. Is it true that immediately Serb forces intervened with your services, firstly, in order to deny all responsibility in this attack; and secondly, to ask urgently establishment of an international investigation commission, mixed. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It is true the Serbs, I think, offered to form a commission to enquire into the origin of this attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, with the assistance of Madam Usher, just before the break, I would like you to have a look at a document P number 137 which is a document which is written in Serbian but that was addressed to you at the time. And in order to make things more simple, there is a translation of the document that was then -- it is on the back of the document. General, do you recognise this document? Have you ever seen it? I am going to ask the question differently. As far as you can recall, was this General Milovanovic who addressed himself to you in relation to this attack?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I have a memory of receiving a letter like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, is it true that at the time, at the same time that Serb forces wanted -- at the time of this attack -- they wanted to have establishment of this investigation commission, international commission, forces of Sarajevo refused this?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It is entirely possible that the United Nations wished to have an independent inquiry, not one made up of both parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, I am going to submit a second document to you in the next 30 seconds with the assistance of Madam Usher, whom I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you asked whether the forces of Sarajevo refused to establish such an international commission --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The response was that it was entirely possible that the United Nations wished to have an independent inquiry --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that might not be an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the reason why I am asking for the document 138 to be submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, same question. You have before you a second letter that was addressed to you again by General Milovanovic. Do you recall this type of document? And do you also know the person, General Ramsey?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I don't remember a General Ramsey. I don't know to whom he would be referring. The normal practice for the Bosnian government was to carry out their own forensic examination on --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, I am going to interrupt you. I am sorry, but the text that you have, perhaps the name is spelled differently. This is Brigadier Ramsey?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Brigadier Ramsey, yes. He was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. So the name that we have here is phonetically written in a different way. So this is Brigadier Ramsey.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President, since we look at the time, we will continue this line of questioning later. Perhaps the witness could be authorised, if that is possible, to have these two documents so that he can read the English translation, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think there is no problem when the witness reads the English translation of these two documents during the break. We will then adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00 and you will have until 20 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, please take the document that I submitted to you a while ago, number 138, and it has to do with General Ramsey. General, do you know whether General Milovanovic had contacted your services immediately following the Markale attack?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he probably did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if you have been in command for such a long time, that it becomes a habit. General, thank you for your assistance. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You see that I know how to obey, General. General, do you know whether it is true that General Milovanovic contacted General Ramsey?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That may have happened. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a no audible response. During the break, the transcriber has made clear to Mr. Piletta-Zanin and myself that where she types "no audible response," there is also no tape record of what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it should then be repeated. We have a "no audible response" on the question whether you -- whether the witness knows that General Milanovic had contacted his services immediately following to the Markale attack and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my question was not reproduced, and we are having a technical problem which does not depend on the speed at which we are speaking. It was simply not registered in the transcript. We must resolve that technical problem, the problem of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a technical problem or is it just -- could I be informed, is there any incident or moment where the transcript could not be prepared as usual? If there is a technical problem, I would like to be informed. There is no technical problem, and since we all are aware that you have sometimes a weaker moment than all your other strong moments, we will then continue and try to locate exactly what we missed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I will do it for you. My question was the following. I cannot always have an eye on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Was it possible that General Milovanovic contacted his counterpart, Brigadier Ramsey, and I believe that the answer given by General Rose was, "It is highly probable." Is that true, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The General's nodding is even more difficult for the transcript. So I see you are nodding "yes." That means that you confirm that the answer as pronounced by Mr. Piletta-Zanin was yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is so. I was waiting for the transcript to finish before I confirmed. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, you have been informed of that document. Is it true that General Milovanovic complained, given the fact that the Muslim forces refused to have a commission, a multi-party commission set up?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. General, now I would like to move on to other subjects. Could you confirm that there was a state of civil war in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am listening, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was addressed to the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- would you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, and this is a political question, it was a civil war, although the Bosnian government did not like it to be referred to as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, did you on your own or by yourself, were you involved in -- were you [In English] not "were you involved." [Interpretation] Did you know about important fighting?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, is it true --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The question as translated into English is: "Did you know about important fighting?" Answer: "Yes." I presume that that is not the question asked by my learned colleague because, if it was, it makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be meaningful if we were -- if Sarajevo were added to the question because it was part of my question. I think that the General answered it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was referring to an important level of conflict taking place in Sarajevo. Was I aware of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer was, "yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did you know about the fact that there was necessarily in Sarajevo -- that there were in Sarajevo necessarily military targets inside or in the centre of civilian areas, of residential areas?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There were certainly military targets, if by that you mean Bosnian government forces stationed within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, I would like you to answer by "yes or no," so as to be clear. Is it true, yes or no, that command and control posts are legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I don't understand the question in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it true, yes or no, that headquarters were legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that roads of a strategic importance or telecommunication means are also the same sort of target?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: If used for military purposes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that cars used by the army for military operations lato sensu were also legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, is it true that in Sarajevo a significant number of such targets, of legitimate military targets, immobile [Realtime transcript read inerror "in mobile"] mainly, were spread through the whole residential are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the transcript or for the translation, the question was: "Immobile" and not "in mobile," I think, in English. This could create confusion. So, therefore, the question was about legitimate military targets, not mobile ones but immobile.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Bosnian government forces were fighting to defend Sarajevo, therefore, they, by definition, were stationed and operating in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, can I understand that your answer is "yes"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am waiting for the transcript. The answer of the witness was, "yes" and it does not appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can I just ask you General to please repeat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...the answer of the witness was, "yes." So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, is it equally true for mobile means, that is to say, military vehicles, transport of troops, transport of mortars, perhaps of tanks, that could circulate around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Certainly, these elements appeared from time to time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And they, therefore, constituted legitimate targets?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Troops moving, or elements of troops moving?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: If these were engaged, that's true, but I have no memory of troops on the move being engaged. Because the positions tended to be static.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, given the time left to me, I would like to ask you a few more questions. Is it true that, to the best of your knowledge, the forces called "Sarajevo forces" had themselves provoked certain interruptions in the electrical supply and in other elements like water and gas?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I think the interruptions from the utilities occurred more from the political than the military side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, you are saying that these were actions emanating more from the political authorities. Does that mean that -- these were the political authorities of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There were occasions when the water supply was cut off when it could have been running and there were occasions when the United Nations engineers were prevented from repairing electricity lines. But usually these difficulties were overcome, and on the whole, we managed to restore electricity and the water for protracted periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, you said "prevent." You meant prevented by the Muslim authorities in Sarajevo? General, do you know --

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It happened occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Again, I have not the answer in the transcript. I am waiting. The answer was -- General, do you know if there was a fund, the source fund, which intervened by bringing money to the Sarajevo authorities to restore the utilities that we have just mentioned, water, electricity, gas, et cetera? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: During that time they concentrated -- the source foundation concentrated on the water restoration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: General, what do you know about how these funds were being used? General, what do you know about how and which way these funds were being used?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There was a water purification plant established in a tunnel, a raid tunnel, to the east of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, I would like to ask you other questions but, in order to do so, I would like to give you, with the assistance of the usher, Exhibit 139, which was copied on the back, as well, for technical -- for technical error, but it is two times the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It bears an "R" number. Is that -- Mr. Ierace, "R" numbers are usually an indication of confidentiality, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You are quite correct, Mr. President, and it may be appropriate to go into closed session because in the time we have left, I probably can't confirm that we have clearance on this document. So to be on the safe side, perhaps we should deal with this in closed court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will then turn into closed session since we are dealing with a document which appears to be confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the damage to Sarajevo occurred before I arrived there and could not have been the consequence of accidental firing. In 1994, the structural damage to the city tended to occur around the areas of confrontation, although, of course, the attack against civilians in Dobrinja and the marketplace caused a much higher loss of life than occurred elsewhere on the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you said that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So there is a difference between structural damage and civilian casualty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you say that the damage that was done before you arrived could not have been accidental damage, that does not answer the question on whether it was not accidental but -- well, let us say intentional at the confrontation lines or intentional away from the confrontation lines. The question was about to make a separation between the damage near to the confrontation lines or further away from the confrontation lines. Your answer was, "It was not accidental," which does not finally answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was talking prior to 1994. Post 1994 when I was there, during 1994, most of the damage to the city tended to be around the conflict line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that before 1994, that damage was mainly -- or at least important damage was also away from the confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for your answer. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise. But the question still doesn't have an answer because, in a sense, what I want to know, if most of the damage, even after the first few years of the conflict, seemed to be near the confrontation lines where combats were. And I don't think that the witness answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness answered the question in that respect. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General you were asked questions in cross-examination about the nature of legitimate military targets, and also whether such targets existed in civilian areas in Sarajevo. What responsibilities does a commander have and what factors should a commander take into account when deciding whether to target a legitimate military object which is situated in a residential area?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The military commander is required to make the maximum effort to prevent civilian casualties, even though the military deployments may be within civilian areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does that decision involve the selection of the type of weaponry to be used when taking out that military object?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It certainly would have a bearing on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And in your opinion, is it appropriate in some circumstances, because of the risk of disproportionate civilian exposure, to forego the opportunity to follow through on a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You were also asked questions as to the intentions of the Serb military leadership during the course of your tenure. The proposition was put to you that the Serbs - I use the words used by the Defence - the Serbs sought, wanted and wished for peace in Sarajevo; to which you replied, "That was generally the case." And earlier you told us that the Serb forces wanted peace because it suited them politically, they controlled 70 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did the Serb leadership, in expressing their desire for peace, ever suggest that they would give up any of the 70 per cent that they had taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to object to this question because it is not at all in respect of the fact that what General Galic is charged with. It is not to find out whether 70 or 80 per cent were under the control of the Serb military authorities elsewhere in Bosnia, but only to find out whether in Sarajevo, whereas General was in charge for his command, whether there was a wish for a campaign, or the contrary, as the General here indicated, that there was a will for peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs could never be described as peacemongers. They were the aggressors. They had taken much of Sarajevo as well as Bosnia. Their reasons for suing for peace in 1994 and trying to develop it from the peace that occurred around Sarajevo to a wider peace in the Balkans, was to take advantage of their military gain. But this does not mean that they were peacemongers. They were not, equally, but the peace agreement around Sarajevo allowed them to withdraw their heavy weapons, required them to withdraw their heavy weapons, which they were able to redeploy to other places such as Gorazde or Bihac, where they were able to intensify the fighting. So a distinction has to be made between a military desire for peace in a particular area and the wider strategic goals, which were to maximise the territorial gains through military victory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You were also asked questions about certain letters that were shown to you from General Milovanovic in the wake of the Markale shelling incident. The thrust of the letters was an offer by the Serb military leadership to partake in a joint investigation with UNPROFOR and with representatives of the Bosnian government army. In the UNPROFOR investigation which did take place, where you told us that experts were brought in, did the Serb military leadership or at least individuals at their -- of their choice within the Serb military, have a role to play in terms of the provision of information and so on?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: With regards to these sorts of attacks, the answer is, we would require them to explain an attack. Usually, they denied it or said that they were responding to Serb attack -- they were responding to Bosnian attacks against them. There was no agreement ever or suggestion, other than from the Serb side, that this Muslim Serb commission should be set up. It would not have been acceptable to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Why is that? Why would it not have been acceptable to the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Because it would have been seen as the United Nations were abdicating their responsibility as an independent mediator to find out the truth of these matters and that the offer of producing a team to go and make an investigation could, of course, been obscuring the truths of who actually fired that bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might the witness be shown two Exhibits P2261 and P2261A. That is the report by UNPROFOR --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecution was complaining that we were not to producing certain exhibits, and we don't have the copies of this and we are unable to follow. I don't know whether Mr. Ierace can have two exhibits because that is what he would have wanted for himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have copies, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have two copies, and this is a matter which arises out of cross-examination which is why I didn't have copies before cross-examination. And the copies I have provided are of the cover sheet of the report proper and one particular page that I will take the witness to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As I was saying earlier, this is a report by UNPROFOR into the Markale -- the report of the Markale investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: General, I think you now have before you two documents, the report proper and the executive summary. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please turn to page, I think it is 46, of the report. It is titled "Annexure G, record of meeting, Bosnian Serb representative, 13 February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Annex G?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "G," yes. If you look towards the top right-hand corner, I think there are handwritten page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The page I am after is 46. So it reads "46-" what appears to be "66" after that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please take a moment to read that to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is it in effect the record of a meeting that took place at Pale on the 13th of February, 1994, between the team leader of the investigation that is, Colonel Gauthier, and some others, and on the other side with Colonel Cvetkovic - I apologise for my pronunciation - who confirmed that he was the Bosnian Serb representative for the purposes of the UN investigation into the Sarajevo market explosion on the 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does the record also note that Colonel Gauthier explained to the Colonel what the team were doing and in what ways Colonel Cvetkovic could contribute to that process, and that included the provision of any physical or technical evidence that he wished to offer the team?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does the record also indicate that indeed there was information provided by the Colonel to the team and that occurred at Lukavica on the 14th of February?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, line 97.8, but we are talking about a Colonel but because we don't see the little sign which is saying it will be checked later, then the name of the Colonel, could Mr. Ierace tell us which Colonel this is and perhaps spell the name because I can see that Colonel Gauthier Realtime transcript read in error "Gortia"] as he is mentioned in the transcript doesn't exist. This is Colonel Gauthier. And if names could be spelled, that would be a great help.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Cvetkovic, and I apologise again for my pronunciation, is C-v-e-t-k-o-v-i-c. Gauthier is G-a-u-t-h-i-e-r and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I have heard that. It is indicated that it will be reviewed by the sign just after the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, there is a name -- word where there is no name. That is the reason why I am intervening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see in the question two Colonels mentioned and then, in the next question, it is Colonel Gauthier explained to the Colonel, and I do understand that is then the other Colonel or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I thought there would be more Colonels. That is the reason why I intervened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In reply to the question, it appears that the Colonel Cvetkovic agreed to produce any possible information, to be handed over at a later date. Whether that happened later, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I direct you to the second last paragraph and, in particular, to the last line, which I think reads: "The latter," that is Colonel Cvetkovic, "agreed to arrange to have such information handed over to the team at Lukavica on 14 February [This occurred at 1600 hours 14 February]"

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, does the report conclude by saying, "Colonel Cvetkovic expressed full satisfaction with the information he had been presented and agreed to communicate with the UNPROFOR LO," for liaison officer, "at Lukavica, should he wish any further contact with the team? The team's representatives departed Pale at 2030 hours."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In other words, was it the case that the Bosnian Serb military, through their nominee, were actively involved at a level of the provision of information, physical items, and also in the sense that they were informed as to the progress and results of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must object to this question, particularly with respect to the way that it was phrased, "actively involved," since it does not appear necessarily in the reading of this text, which is -- which implies active involvement as to this operation, and this phrasing seems too direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am happy to rephrase the question, to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because we are having a -- in the beginning of the morning, someone thought that we might have time available today. We certainly have not. So if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does the report reflect, to the best of your recollection, the degree of involvement of the Bosnian Serb military, through their nominee, in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a few more questions. It may be that if Your Honours have questions that we need to go over, but I could probably finish in the matter of a few minutes very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I do not know -- this courtroom will be used at a quarter past 2.00. So it is unfortunately -- how much time would you still need? And would the interpreters be ready to -- if it is a matter of a couple of minutes, but let me just first confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I am afraid it will not be able to finish today, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a difficulty for that because I have to leave on the airplane for other commitments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would mean that we have to, first of all, ask the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could assist. I will forego any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if the interpreters could assist us for a couple of more minutes, because there are a few questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, no problem, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We might be able to conclude today, which is highly preferable, apart from whether it is possible at all. So I will then give an opportunity to Judge Nieto-Navia to put a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I have only one question about the blue routes, because you said that they were used by the UN convoys for transporting the humanitarian aid, I suppose, but we have some evidence that they were used for people -- people were using the blue routes for entering or going out of the city. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That is not true. The only people who went in and out of the city on the blue routes were elderly people going from Sarajevo to Zenica and back. I think every Tuesday there was a bus which passed an inspection first by the Bosnian government people and then by the Serbs and, they were allowed through. And there was a very limited movement across of injured civilians from time to time. But that is the only routine passage of civilians across that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi as the one or more questions for you also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like you please, very briefly, to ask you to clarify for me two points, the first being that I wanted to know whether you rule out the possibility that the nonfunctioning of public services was caused by the attacks. What I understood it, occasionally, the nonfunctioning was caused by operations of the government, actions of the government, of the local authorities. Do you rule out that they were damaged by the firing or the attacks of the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: Both situations occurred. Sometimes they were destroyed by exchange of fire, sometimes by deliberate obstruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, I would just like you to tell us about the events that took place on the 5th of February known as "Markale market." I am not asking you who is responsible for it, which side, but this event, as a fact, is that true or is it set up, made up, planted by the media -- for the media for propaganda purposes?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: No, this situation, this event, occurred in all the reality that were then reported by the media. It is a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Then as far as you know, were there wounded, people killed, or no one was killed, no one was touched?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: There were 58 people killed and some hundred people injured in that attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have two questions for you. The first, you told us about the answer General Mladic gave on your complaints about the use of weaponry. The answer was that the BiH forces had far more infantry and, therefore, as I understand it, the Bosnian Serbs would use their fire power, shelling, artillery. No, shelling. You could understand this answer in two different ways. The first is that you would shell where the infantry was concentrated, and another understanding of such answer would be that you would shell wherever in order to stop the infantry moving forward, even if they were at the front lines and not where the shelling took place. Which of the two understandings of General Mladic's answer would be the correct one, or is there even a third?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: General Mladic didn't specify what targets he was engaging in response to infantry attack. He merely said: "Our response to infantry attack is shelling," the implication being shelling either against the infantry themselves or other wider targets elsewhere, including possibly civilians, although he did not specify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you understood it to be not limited to shelling infantry concentrations? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: That was the implication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second question is: You told us that sniping took place from both sides. Was there any difference in targets? I mean, sniping can be directed against civilian individuals or military individuals. Was the sniping, in every respect, the same from both sides?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: The level of sniping was definitely greater by the Serbs. The targets being engaged on both sides, civilian casualties occurred because of the sniping. But again, the greater number of civilians killed were obviously the Bosnians within the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you talking about the relative numbers or the -- I mean percentages or numbers as such?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL ROSE
utterances.text: I would say that the number translates in the percentages. The greater number of sniper incidents were by the Bosnian Serb Army into Sarajevo which included civilian casualties, although there were cases of civilian casualties being caused on the Serb side by the Bosnian forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for your clarification. This then concludes your testimony in this court, Sir Michael. May I thank you very much for coming, and I hope you get your plane, that we didn't keep you too long in this courtroom. It is important for us to hear the answers to questions of both parties and the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, apologise. I was asked by General Galic. Who wanted very exceptionally just to ask one question. He has asked me to ask. This is literally in 30 seconds. The question is if General Rose knew that Serb civilians also lived in Sarajevo where they held their territory, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He is permitted to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbs lived in Sarajevo as well. In Grbavica and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes, finally, your testimony in this court. Once again, thank you very much and I hope you get your plane. Madam Usher, could you please escort Sir Michael out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I respectfully suggest that the Prosecution would have no objection to the exhibits being tendered tomorrow morning, if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is certainly a suggestion that I would only be too glad to follow. But I have got two questions -- one question and one remark. Tomorrow, we'll hear the testimony of and cross-examination of the expert Zecevic. The Chamber has decided that the cross-examination certainly will not have to take more than two hours. So that is the time limit imposed upon the Defence. And then my last question is in respect of the witnesses under Rule 92 bis (C). You told us that one of the witnesses would be withdrawn. I haven't seen anything yet. Could you indicate for which witness you are going to submit further information and which witness you will withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Lindre will be withdrawn, and we are preparing some submissions which will be filed tomorrow in relation to the balance, and those submissions simply consider the impact of the recent Appeals Chamber judgment to the extent that that judgment states some principles of general application, 7-1 and 7-3 cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I was talking about 92 bis (C), that is Bajram Sopi and Cavcic. There must be some follow up, I think, and I thought that you would withdraw that -- one of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, I am sorry, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a misunderstanding. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is just to clarify things. If tomorrow we have the possibility of having our expert here in the courtroom at the time of the examination-in-chief of Mr. Zecevic tomorrow, it goes without saying that we will have to ask for time after the examination-in-chief because it doesn't serve to anything if we have an expert and if we cannot listen to what he -- his opinion and what he has heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will get the necessary time. But Mr. Zecevic is introduced as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But he will testify, it is not just the report submitted? What could we expect?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the evidence in chief will be very brief. I expect it will be taken in the time taken by Robert Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that is at least clear to us. Then I think especially the interpreters who have hard times these days, I am fully aware of that, for their assistance and for granting us another quarter of an hour. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before you rise for the day, I have in mind. If I could say this cryptically, some comments that you made yesterday or the day before about the need from time to time to intervene. That may apply tomorrow, in terms of limiting appropriately, and in that way assisting with witnesses. I simply indicate that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 21st day of June, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
